newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Renault move tough but needed - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Renault move tough but needed - analysts.

text.p: French carmaker Renault's drives to cut costs by eliminating nearly 6,000 jobs should help restore the company's car operations to profitability, industry analysts said on Wednesday.

But they said the outcry provoked by the closure of a Belgian plant employing 3,100 workers and the reduction of nearly 2,800 jobs in France signalled that Renault's management faces huge constraints even though its recovery is hardly assured.

They said Renault also needs to restructure its truck-making business, which includes Mack Trucks of the United States and which is expected to show a 1996 operating loss of at least 600 million francs.

Chairman Louis Schweitzer is scheduled to meet Prime Minister Juppe this afternoon to defend his decisions which have been criticised by unions, opposition politicians and the government, its biggest shareholder with 46 percent.

"Even the fact that he's meeting Juppe, to an international investor, doesn't have a good feel about it," said analyst John Lawson at Salomon Brothers. He said the meeting raised questions "whether he's (Schweitzer) a free man, if he ever was".

Renault was partly privatised in 1994 and the state reduced its stake to below 50 percent last summer. The company recently cautioned that it expects a big loss for 1996. Analysts estimate a loss of five billion francs or more, including charges for the Belgian plant closure and French job cuts.
Lawson said the moves announced by Renault were positive and were likely to tip the group "to the right side of zero".
"But if that's all, I'd be disappointed...they've got to balance it across the group, into their commercial vehicles too," he said.

Schweitzer told reporters at the Geneva car show on Tuesday that the restructuring of the car assembly operations in Europe, including the Belgian plant closure, would result in savings of 850 million francs. He said that was a conservative estimate.
Analyst Keith Hayes at Goldman Sachs said he estimated the restructuring and the job cuts in France would save two billion francs, but that barely compensates for the car division's operating loss.

"It's possible these savings will get them back to break-even," he said. "Renault's management is constrained on all sides. This is just a start, and already they're running into political interference. This highlights the almost impossible situation the management is in," he said.
"This is not about rewarding shareholders, who have suffered a tremendous loss. This is about preservation," he said.

Analysts say Renault's decisions were necessary given the weak growth expected in the European car market, the fall in sales expected to exceed 10 percent this year in France, and a price war that has made it difficult for any carmaker to earn money in Europe.
Renault, the smallest of the six volume carmakers in Europe, is in a particularly precarious position because of its heavy dependence on the French and European markets.
"Car companies are doing all they can to limit the negative impact of the industrial structure in Europe," Hayes said.
The European industry's overcapacity is estimated at 20 percent or more and for a variety of reasons, political and nationalistic, consolidation is not expected to occur soon.

Several analysts said the stock's ups and downs in recent days reflect concerns that Renault may back down on its plans. But analysts in both Paris and London said they did not believe Renault would retreat or that the government would push it to do so despite political criticism of the abrupt manner of the announcements.
"I think they're going to back Schweitzer," said one analyst. "They can't say, 'Don't close the plant' -- full stop. If they do that, they have to engineer another plan, possibly a merger."

One Paris-based analyst said he thought Renault's moves were very encouraging. "It's a sign the group is conscious of its problems. These measures are more energetic than what we've seen up to now," he said.

He added that the measures appeared to have the fingerprints of Carlos Ghosn, who formerly headed and restructured tyremaker Michelin's North American operations before coming to Renault recently in a senior position.
